extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and administrative patent judges; patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Revised USPTO examination procedure for determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), focusing on revised Step 2A (two-prong test) and related Step 2B (inventive concept) analysis applied to patent claims across technology centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations: mathematical formulas as such are not patentable; claims that are a series of mathematical calculations or organizing information through mathematical correlations are abstract. Use case law (e.g., Bilski, Benson, Diehr, SAP v. InvestPic, Digitech) to identify mathematical-concept abstract ideas. Note that use of generic computer components does not necessarily remove a claim from this grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing, sales activities); business relations; managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from case law: hedging, offer-based price optimization, creating contractual relationships, marketing/sales processes, and organizational/management methods. If a claim limitation recites these concepts per se, treat it as an abstract idea. Improvements to how such activities are performed (e.g., technological improvements) may render a claim eligible at step one if the claim integrates the idea into a practical application or improves computer/technology functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind (including observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, a claim covers performance in the mind (except where claim cannot practically be performed mentally), classify it as a mental-process abstract idea. Generic computer-implementation language does not remove a claim from this grouping if the steps could be performed mentally or with pen and paper. Case citations: Mortg. Grader, Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec, CyberSource, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims not reciting enumerated abstract-idea groupings should generally not be treated as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that do not recite matter that falls within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas, except in rare circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner believes a limitation outside enumerated groupings nonetheless constitutes an abstract idea, follow the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (see Section III.C). Use the enumerated groupings in Section I as the primary reference instead of prior Quick Reference Sheets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed subject matter falls within one of the four statutory categories identified by 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This check is unchanged by the 2019 guidance. Examiners may use the existing streamlined analyses (Pathway A) where patent eligibility is self-evident. Passing Step 1 does not end patentability analysis—claims must still satisfy 102, 103, and 112, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised Step 2A: Prong One — Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One evaluates whether the claim recites a judicial exception: a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (as grouped in Section I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites an exception, proceed to Prong Two. If not, claim is eligible at Prong One and analysis concludes (unless rare circumstances). Use the Section I groupings to determine whether a claimed concept is an abstract idea rather than comparing to prior Quick Reference Sheets or a case-by-case list. For laws of nature and natural phenomena, continue to follow MPEP 2106.04(b) and (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised Step 2A: Prong Two — Is the recited judicial exception integrated into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two evaluates whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. If integrated, the claim is not 'directed to' the judicial exception and is eligible at Prong Two (concluding analysis). If not integrated, the claim is 'directed to' the exception and proceeds to Step 2B. Examples of integration: improvements to computer functioning or other technology/technological field (cases: Enfish, McRO, Core Wireless, BASCOM, DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Inventive-concept inquiry (does the claim provide 'significantly more'?)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2A, evaluate whether the additional elements individually or in combination provide an inventive concept — i.e., whether they amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether additional elements: (a) add a specific limitation or combination not well-understood, routine, conventional in the field (indicative of an inventive concept), or (b) simply append well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level (indicative of no inventive concept). A determination that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional must be supported by factual findings (see Berkheimer memorandum). Reevaluate any elements previously considered 'insignificant extra-solution activity' when performing Step 2B because they may be unconventional in combination (examples: data-gathering steps that are performed unconventionally). If the additional elements amount to significantly more, the claim is eligible; otherwise reject for lack of subject-matter eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual support requirement for conventionality findings (Berkheimer considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions that an additional element or combination is 'well-understood, routine, conventional' must be supported with a factual determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should provide factual support (and may rely on specification disclosure or external evidence) when asserting that a limitation is conventional. If facts indicate the limitation is unconventional, that may support finding an inventive concept at Step 2B (e.g., Exergen temperature-detection example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of claim limitations not falling in enumerated groupings: 'Tentative abstract idea' procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare circumstances, if an examiner believes a claim limitation not in Section I should be treated as an abstract idea (a 'tentative abstract idea'), follow prescribed procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application; if not integrated, evaluate additional elements for inventive concept under Step 2B. If the examiner concludes the claim is ineligible based on treating a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea, the Technology Center Director must approve the rejection and a justification must be recorded in the file. Similarly, PTAB panels that treat a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea should seek PTAB leadership clearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluation of earlier 'insignificant' findings during Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should reevaluate conclusions made in Prong Two (Step 2A) about elements being insignificant extra-solution activity when performing Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An element judged insignificant in Step 2A may, upon reevaluation, be found unconventional or unconventional in combination and thus constitute an inventive concept at Step 2B (example: unconventional data-gathering steps may render a claim eligible at Step 2B even if not integrated at Step 2A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution and concurrent analysis of other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a Section 101 rejection, a complete examination should be made for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compact prosecution does not mandate the order of analysis. Examiners must avoid confusing requirements of other statutes with the Section 101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance scope and effect (administrative policy—not substantive rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: This 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance sets agency policy for interpretation of Section 101 and supersedes prior USPTO internal materials to the extent inconsistent; it does not constitute substantive rulemaking and does not have the force of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is to be followed by USPTO personnel as an internal management tool; failure by personnel to follow it is not itself a proper basis for appeal or petition. Rejections remain based on substantive law and are appealable to PTAB and courts. The guidance supersedes MPEP 2106.04(II) insofar as that portion equated 'reciting' with 'directed to', and supersedes prior 'Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet' versions.
